newsitem.title: USA: Reno seen rejecting independent fund-raising probe.
newsitem.headline: Reno seen rejecting independent fund-raising probe.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno is expected to reject an independent counsel for the campaign fund-raising controversy on Monday, arguing that the Justice Department's investigation should go on without interruption.

Reno is due to respond to a request from congressional Republicans that she take the first step toward an independent counsel to investigate allegations of improper Democratic fund-raising to help President Bill Clinton in the 1996 campaign.
"From everything I have heard, Reno will turn them down," a senior Justice Department official said of the request from Republicans on the House and Senate Judiciary committees.
The official said the attorney general had relied heavily on the advice of career Justice Department officials for her decision.

Clinton and Reno both maintained an independent counsel was unwarranted, even though allegations have continued to mount involving the role of the president, Vice President Al Gore and White House officials in raising campaign funds.

Sen. Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch said in the request to Reno that an independent counsel should probe fund-raising activities at the White House and possibly illegal foreign contributions from people associated with the Lippo Group, a financial conglomerate based in Indonesia.

Reno repeatedly has taken the position that the threshold under the independent counsel law -- specific evidence from a credible source that a covered individual has committed a crime -- has not been reached.
An aide to Reno said he was unaware of any developments that have changed her mind ahead of Monday's formal response.
Reno also has promised to seek the appointment of an outside counsel to take over the investigation only if the required evidence of wrongdoing is found.
In the meantime, she has vowed a thorough and aggressive investigation by a Justice Department task force consisting of career prosecutors from its public integrity unit and more than 30 FBI agents.
"The attorney general is personally supervising that investigation," Acting Deputy Attorney General Seth Waxman told reporters on Thursday.
Justice Department officials said switching to an independent counsel could cause unnecessary delays and complications for the investigation.

"It would bring the investigation to a screeching halt," one official said, adding that task force no longer could use the grand jury to hear testimony, could not issue any more subpoenas and could not grant immunity to witnesses.

More time would be lost waiting for the special three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals to appoint the counsel and then for the prosecutor to hire staff and begin operations, the officials said.
They said the far-flung investigation so far:

-- is focusing on former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang, a key figure in the foreign-money controversy; Little Rock restauranteur Charles Trie, who raised hundreds of thousands of dollars for the Democrats in the 1996 campaign; and Johnny Chung, a Taiwanese American who gave $366,000 to the Democrats that had to be returned.
-- is looking into allegations that China, directly or indirectly, sought to funnel campaign contributions to the Democratic Party or to congressional candidates. China has denied the allegations.

-- heard testimony from a lobbyist for Pakistan who alleged that Rep. Dan Burton, a Republican leading a House probe into campaign fund-raising abuses, had shaken him down for contributions for his re-election campaign last year.
-- heard testimony from a Florida businessman about his talks in October with Clinton and then-White House Deputy Chief of Staff Harold Ickes about a possible campaign contribution.
